turns.prompt_text: in Fish Shell, I'm riding a for loop, but I can't finish it. How do I finish the for loop?
turns.response_html:
To finish a for loop in Fish shell, you simply use the end keyword.

Unlike Bash, which uses done, or Python, which relies on indentation, Fish uses a straightforward block-based syntax. Here is the structure:

The Basic Syntax

for variable in list
    # Your commands go here
end

Examples of Closing the Loop

  • Iterating over a range of numbers:

    for i in (seq 1 5)
    echo "Value: $i"
end

  • Iterating over files in a directory:

    for file in *.jpg
    echo "Processing $file"
end

  • A quick one-liner: If you are typing directly into the terminal, you can write it all on one line by using semicolons: for i in 1 2 3; echo $i; end

Why it might feel "stuck"

If you are typing this in an interactive terminal and the prompt hasn't returned to normal, it’s usually because Fish is waiting for that end keyword.

  1. Type end and hit Enter.
  2. If you realized you made a mistake and want to cancel the loop entirely without finishing it, press Ctrl+C.

turns.prompt_text: I'm using a string to split the name of a PDF. It's named in a convention of chapter number.extension. I want to remove the period and extension from the end of the text.
turns.response_html:
To strip the extension and the period in Fish, the most efficient tool is the string builtin. Since Fish is designed to be helpful and readable, it offers a few different ways to handle this depending on how specific your filename pattern is.

The Most Direct Method: string replace

If you want to specifically target the .pdf (or any extension) and replace it with nothing, use:

set filename "01.pdf"
set chapter (string replace -r '\.pdf$' '' $filename)
echo $chapter
  • -r: This enables Regular Expressions.
  • \.pdf$: This matches a literal period followed by "pdf" only at the end of the string.
  • '': This tells Fish to replace that match with "nothing."

The "Cleanest" Method: string split

If your files always follow the number.extension format, you can split the string at the period and take only the first part:

set filename "05.pdf"
set chapter (string split -m 1 . $filename)[1]
echo $chapter
  • -m 1: This tells Fish to stop splitting after the first period (useful if you have files like 01.v2.pdf).
  • [1]: Fish arrays are 1-indexed, so this selects the first part (the number).

The Robust Method: basename

If you are iterating through a list of files in a loop, the standard Unix command basename is often the most readable way to strip a known extension:

for file in *.pdf
    set chapter (basename $file .pdf)
    echo "Processing Chapter: $chapter"
end

Integration into your Loop

Since you were working on a for loop, here is how you might put it all together to rename or process those files:

for file in *.pdf
    # Strip the .pdf extension
    set chapter (string replace -r '\.pdf$' '' $file)
    
    # Optional: If you also want to remove the period from "01."
    set clean_name (string replace "." "" $chapter)
    
    echo "The chapter number is $clean_name"
end

turns.prompt_text: Can string do two things at the same time? I'm doing a split with string as well.
turns.response_html:
In Fish, the string command is incredibly versatile, but it follows a linear logic—it processes input and gives you an output. While it can't technically perform two different operations (like a split and a regex replace) in a single "step," you can pipe multiple string commands together to achieve a complex result in one line.

If you are trying to split the string and clean up the extension at the same time, piping is your best friend.

The "One-Liner" Pipe Method

If your filename is 01.pdf and you want to split by the period but also ensure the result is clean, you can chain them:

set filename "01.pdf"
set chapter (string split "." $filename | string match -v "pdf")
echo $chapter
  • string split ".": Breaks 01.pdf into two lines: 01 and pdf.
  • | (The Pipe): Passes those two lines to the next command.
  • string match -v "pdf": The -v flag means "invert match" (keep everything except "pdf").

Using Regex for "Two-in-One"

If you want to do a "split-like" action and a "remove" action simultaneously, string replace -r (regex) is the most powerful way. It can look for a pattern and return only the part you want:

set filename "01.pdf"
# Match the digits before a period, and ignore the rest
set chapter (string replace -r '^(\d+)\..*' '$1' $filename)
  • ^(\d+): Capture the digits at the start.
  • \..*: Match the period and everything after it.
  • '$1': Replace the whole string with only the captured digits.

Handling Multiple Splits

If your filename is more complex (e.g., Chapter.01.pdf) and you want to split and extract a specific part:

set filename "Chapter.01.pdf"
# Split by period, and pick the second item (the number)
set chapter (string split "." $filename)[2]

Which approach fits your file names best?

If your file looks like...Use this string combo
01.pdf`string split -m 1 . $file
Chapter_01.pdfstring replace -r '.*_(\d+)\..*' '$1'
01.v2.pdfstring split "." $file (then pick the index)

Would you like me to show you how to wrap this into a "dry run" loop so you can see the results before you actually rename or move any files?

In Fish shell, the -r flag stands for Regular Expressions (regex).

By default, string commands like replace or match look for literal text. When you add -r, you unlock a powerful pattern-matching language that allows you to describe types of text (like "any digit" or "anything at the start of a line") rather than just specific characters.

Why use -r instead of a normal string?

Imagine you have a file named Chapter.01.pdf.

  • Without -r (Literal): string replace ".pdf" "" "Chapter.01.pdf" This only works if the file ends exactly in .pdf. If the file is .PDF or .jpg, it fails.

  • With -r (Regex): string replace -r '\..*$' '' "Chapter.01.pdf" This says: "Find a literal period (\.), then match every character after it (.*) until the end of the line ($), and delete it." This works for any extension.

Common Regex Symbols in Fish

When you use -r, you can use these special operators:

SymbolMeaningExample
^Start of the string^01 (matches "01" only at the beginning)
$End of the stringpdf$ (matches "pdf" only at the very end)
\dAny digit (0-9)\d+ (matches one or more numbers)
.Any single charactera.c (matches "abc", "a2c", "a!c")
\.A literal period(Necessary because . usually means "anything")
*Zero or more of the previous thing\d* (matches any amount of digits)

The "Capture Group" Superpower

The most advanced thing -r does is allow you to "capture" part of a string and reuse it. You wrap the part you want to keep in parentheses ().

set file "Chapter_22.pdf"

# We want the '22'
# Regex: find 'Chapter_', capture digits (\d+), ignore '.pdf'
# Then replace the whole thing with the captured group '$1'
set result (string replace -r 'Chapter_(\d+)\.pdf' '$1' $file)

echo $result  # Output: 22

A Quick Tip for Fish

If you aren't sure if your regex is correct, you can test it with string match -r: string match -r '\d+' "Chapter 42" If it returns "42", your pattern is working!

turns.prompt_text: Given text like `./pdf-raw/Chapter 8.pdf`, where the number stays in the single digit, how can I save only that number to a variable
turns.response_html:
To extract just the digit from a path like ./pdf-raw/Chapter 8.pdf in Fish, you can use the string command with a regular expression (-r) to "capture" exactly what you need.

Since you are dealing with a path, a filename, and an extension, here is the most reliable way to isolate that single digit:

The "Capture Group" Method

This method looks for a digit surrounded by other text and "extracts" it into your variable.

set file "./pdf-raw/Chapter 8.pdf"

# This matches any digit (\d) and saves it
set chapter_num (string replace -r '.*(\d)\.pdf$' '$1' $file)

echo $chapter_num
# Output: 8

Breaking Down the Regex Pattern

To understand how string -r is performing this "surgery" on your text, here is the breakdown:

  • .*: Matches everything at the start (the ./pdf-raw/Chapter part).
  • (\d): The parentheses create a capture group. \d specifically looks for a single digit. Because it is in parentheses, Fish remembers it as $1.
  • \.pdf$: Matches the literal period and "pdf" at the very end of the string.
  • '$1': This is the "replacement" argument. It tells Fish: "Throw away everything you matched and replace it with only the content of the first capture group (the digit)."

An Alternative: string match

If you prefer not to "replace" text and just want to "find" the digit, string match is often more intuitive:

set file "./pdf-raw/Chapter 8.pdf"
set chapter_num (string match -r '\d' $file)

Note: This works perfectly as long as there are no other numbers in the folder path (like pdf-raw2). If your path has other numbers, stick to the string replace method above which is more specific.

Putting it into your Loop

Here is how it looks fully integrated into the loop you were building:

for file in ./pdf-raw/*.pdf
    set chapter_num (string replace -r '.*(\d)\.pdf$' '$1' $file)
    echo "Processing Chapter: $chapter_num"
    # Do your work here...
end

turns.prompt_text: No, thank you. In Phish, my terminal looks like this: `austinrognes@Austins-Mac-mini ~/D/S/Intro-to-Electronics>` How can I succinctify this?
turns.response_html:
In Fish (often playfully called "Phish"), your prompt is controlled by a function called fish_prompt. By default, it shows your full user@hostname and a long directory path, which can quickly crowd your screen.

To "succinctify" this, you have two main options: the Quick & Visual way or the Manual & Minimal way.

Option 1: The Quick Way (fish_config)

Fish has a built-in web-based configuration tool that lets you pick a new prompt style visually.

  1. Type fish_config prompt in your terminal.
  2. Your browser will open a page showing dozens of prompt styles.
  3. Look for "Classic", "Informative", or "Lean" styles that use ~ or just the current folder name.
  4. Click Use Prompt and it will save automatically.

Option 2: The Manual Way (Custom Function)

If you want total control—for example, removing the user@hostname and shortening the path—you can rewrite the prompt function.

Run this command in your terminal to see a "succinct" version immediately:

function fish_prompt
    set_color blue
    echo -n (prompt_pwd)
    set_color normal
    echo -n " > "
end
  • prompt_pwd: This is a built-in Fish magic trick. It automatically turns ~/Documents/School/Intro-to-Electronics into ~/D/S/Intro-to-Electronics.
  • echo -n: The -n tells Fish not to start a new line, so your typing stays on the same line as the prompt.

How to Make it Permanent

If you like the manual version above, you need to save it so it survives a restart:

  1. Create the functions directory if it doesn't exist: mkdir -p ~/.config/fish/functions
  2. Save the function to a file: funcsave fish_prompt

A "Pro" Succinct Tip

If you want to keep the path but hide that long austinrognes@Austins-Mac-mini part, you can use the "Hydro" or "Pure" styles. They usually only show the current folder:

Intro-to-Electronics >

Instead of:

austinrognes@Austins-Mac-mini ~/D/S/Intro-to-Electronics>

Would you like me to help you add a specific feature to your prompt, like showing the current Git branch or changing the color based on whether the last command failed?

To make your Fish prompt both succinct and powerful, we can modify your fish_prompt function to include two of the most helpful "pro" features: Git integration (so you know which branch you are on) and Status colors (so the prompt turns red if a command fails).

The "Succinct & Smart" Prompt

Copy and paste this into your terminal to see it in action:

function fish_prompt
    set -l last_status $status
    
    # 1. Show the shortened directory path (~/D/S/Intro-to-Electronics)
    set_color blue
    echo -n (prompt_pwd)

    # 2. Show Git branch if inside a repository
    set_color yellow
    printf '%s ' (fish_git_prompt)

    # 3. Change the arrow color to red if the last command failed
    if test $last_status -eq 0
        set_color green
    else
        set_color red
    end

    echo -n " ❯ "
    set_color normal
end

Why this is better:

  • Contextual Awareness: It hides your user@hostname entirely, giving you back about 30 characters of screen space.
  • Visual Feedback: If you type a command that doesn't work (like a typo), the ❯ will turn red, letting you know there was an error without you having to check.
  • Git Status: If you are working on code or school projects in a Git folder, it will automatically show (main) or (branch-name) next to the folder.

How to Save This Permanently

If you like how this looks and want to keep it every time you open your Mac's terminal:

  1. Type funcsave fish_prompt and hit Enter.
  2. Fish will automatically create the file at ~/.config/fish/functions/fish_prompt.fish for you.

Bonus: Adding a Timestamp

Since you mentioned you like gathering perspectives and information from various sources, sometimes it's helpful to know when you ran a specific experiment or command. You can add a small timestamp to the right side of your terminal (the RPROMPT) so it doesn't clutter your main typing line:

function fish_right_prompt
    set_color 555 # This is a dim grey
    date "+%H:%M:%S"
    set_color normal
end

# Save it if you like it:
funcsave fish_right_prompt

turns.prompt_text: alright, how do I activate this? I've got it saved.
turns.response_html:
Since you have already used funcsave, Fish has written that code into a specific file in your configuration folder (~/.config/fish/functions/fish_prompt.fish).

Because Fish autoloads functions, it should technically be active the next time you open a terminal window. However, to see the changes right now in your current session, you have two quick options:

1. The "Source" Command (Instant Refresh)

Tell Fish to re-read its function file immediately:

source ~/.config/fish/functions/fish_prompt.fish

The moment you hit Enter, your prompt should transform into the succinct version we built.

2. The "New Shell" Method

If you want to verify that it's truly "permanent," simply type:

exec fish

This replaces your current shell process with a fresh one. If your prompt looks correct here, it means you've successfully saved it for all future sessions.

Troubleshooting

If the prompt didn't change, or if it looks "broken" (e.g., showing raw code instead of a prompt), check these two things:

  • Syntax Check: Ensure the word function fish_prompt is at the very top of the file and end is at the very bottom.
  • File Name: Fish is picky—the file must be named exactly fish_prompt.fish inside the ~/.config/fish/functions/ folder.

Pro-Tip: If you ever want to go back to the default "Long" prompt, just delete that file:
rm ~/.config/fish/functions/fish_prompt.fish

turns.prompt_text: It is not showing only the current folder. This is what it's showing. `~/D/S/Intro-to-Electronics ❯ `
turns.response_html:
Ah, I see! You want it even more succinct—specifically, you want it to hide the "parent" folders and only show the folder you are currently inside (the "basename").

The prompt_pwd function we used earlier is designed to shorten paths like ~/Documents/School to ~/D/S, but it won't hide them entirely. To show only Intro-to-Electronics, we need to change one line in your function.

The Fix

Run this in your terminal to update the function:

function fish_prompt
    set -l last_status $status
    
    # 1. Show ONLY the current folder name
    set_color blue
    echo -n (basename (pwd))

    # 2. Show Git branch
    set_color yellow
    printf '%s ' (fish_git_prompt)

    # 3. Status color for the arrow
    if test $last_status -eq 0
        set_color green
    else
        set_color red
    end

    echo -n " ❯ "
    set_color normal
end

What changed?

  • Instead of (prompt_pwd), we are using (basename (pwd)).
    • pwd gets the full path.
    • basename strips everything away except the very last folder name.

How to apply and save it:

Since you’ve already saved a version, you just need to overwrite it:

  1. Paste the code above into your terminal and hit Enter.
  2. Type funcsave fish_prompt to save this new "ultra-succinct" version.
  3. Type source ~/.config/fish/functions/fish_prompt.fish to refresh.

Now, your prompt should look like this: Intro-to-Electronics ❯

One small catch: If you are in your home directory, basename might show your username (e.g., austinrognes) instead of the ~ symbol. Does that work for you, or would you like it to show ~ when you're at the root of your home folder?
